reading.rtitle: The Company That Learned to Explain Itself
paras: Ana Beltrán has run the same company for twelve years, and for the first nine of them almost nobody outside Madrid could say what it did. Vantia is a consultancy — a hundred and forty people who go inside client companies and rebuild the way those companies use their own numbers. She has never sold software, and she says she has never wanted to. What changed in year ten was not the work. It was the sentence.

The sentence came out of a bad meeting. A German buyer had flown in for the afternoon, and Ana talked for eleven minutes about architecture, migrations and the AI-driven models her team had built. At the end the buyer asked, politely, what the company actually sold. “I had given him everything except the answer,” she says. “I have told that story a hundred times since, always against myself.” She went home that night and wrote one line: Vantia rebuilds how mid-sized companies use their own data, and we have done it a hundred and eighty times.

That line does three things at once, and she has kept all three ever since. It names the work. It names the size — a hundred and eighty projects is a track record, and a track record is the only argument a buyer cannot argue with. And it leaves out everything else: the portfolio of internal tools, the awards, the map. Vantia is headquartered in Madrid and has opened two offices since, in Lisbon and in Milan, but Ana no longer opens with geography. “Nobody has ever bought a company because of where its office is,” she says.

The next milestone is the one she has been avoiding for years. A consultancy grows by hiring, which means it is not scalable the way a software business is, and every investor who has looked at Vantia has said so inside the first hour. Ana has spent two years building a product layer on top of the consulting work, precisely so that the company can scale up without doubling the number of people it employs. It has not shipped yet. Two firms have made offers and she has turned both down, which she is careful to describe as timing rather than principle.

What she says she has learned is narrower, and more useful, than a lesson about selling a company. “For nine years I thought that explaining the company was marketing, and that marketing was somebody else’s job,” she says. “It is not. It is the job. If the founder cannot say it in one sentence, nobody further down is going to say it better.”

listenings.text: Sixty seconds, so I am going to skip the part everybody skips anyway. We have been operating for nine years. There are a hundred and ten of us. We have done two hundred and forty deployments, and I am not going to put a final number on a slide because that number goes up every single month, which is the only interesting thing about it. What I am not going to talk about is the technology. I have been in this room before and I have watched founders spend their whole slot on an architecture diagram, and I have never once seen anybody write a cheque because of one. So here is what I will say instead. We have never lost a client to a competitor. Not one, in nine years. Ask me about that and I will use the rest of my time on it.

A track record proves exactly one thing, and founders consistently ask it to prove two. It proves that you can repeat what you have already done. Two hundred projects means the two hundred and first is low risk, and that is genuinely valuable. What it does not prove, and what no number of past projects will ever prove, is that you can do something you have never done. That is why the first question every investor asks a consultancy is whether it is scalable, and in my experience it comes inside the first hour, usually inside the first twenty minutes. Here is what I tell founders. Answer that question before it is asked, and answer it with a number. A founder who waits to be asked looks like a founder who has not thought about it, and that impression is very expensive and almost impossible to undo later.

extra_audio.text: Dataside has been operating for fifteen years. We are headquartered in Sao Jose dos Campos, and we opened our second office in 2018. We have delivered more than four hundred projects since we started. We have never lost a client to a competitor. We have not launched the product layer yet, but we have been building it for two years. And you, what would you need to see to take the next meeting?
